topic: What if you woke up in the year 3000?

script.text: At first, it's just a sneeze. Then a fever. By night, you can't get out of bed.
Vee scans you. 'This is a common cold. Children here catch it and feel nothing.'

Here's the problem. Viruses never stop changing. The flu changes so much that scientists make a new flu vaccine every single year. Your body learned to fight the germs of twenty twenty-six. It has never seen almost a thousand years of new ones.

It has happened before. After fourteen ninety-two, diseases from Europe reached the Americas, where nobody had immunity. Within about a century, in many places, around nine out of ten people had died.
Vee gives you a shot that fixes you in an hour. Without the future's medicine, that little cold could have been the end of you.

Some things barely change. Earth's spin is slowing down, so the day gets about two thousandths of a second longer every century. After nine hundred and seventy-four years, your day is longer by about seventeen thousandths of a second. That's the one change you will never notice.
Then comes the next problem. Talking. Without your earpiece, nobody understands a word you say.

That's real too. English changes all the time. Beowulf was written in English about a thousand years ago, and today almost nobody can read it without lessons. It starts with the word 'Hwaet.' To the people of the year three thousand, you sound just as strange.
And then, the worst one. Work. Your seven days of credit are almost gone, and the tours are getting old.
You look for a job. Every job you know how to do is done by machines.
That happened to your great-grandparents too. In nineteen hundred, about four in ten American workers worked on farms. By the year two thousand, it was fewer than two in a hundred.
In the year three thousand, your skills are like a horse and cart. Fun to look at. Useless.
And that's when someone else starts paying attention.

science.claim: Influenza viruses change constantly (antigenic drift), so the flu vaccine is reviewed and updated every year.
science.working: Small mutations in the flu virus's surface proteins add up each season; WHO meets twice a year to recommend the strains for the next vaccine.
science.source: CDC, 'How the Flu Virus Can Change: Drift and Shift'; WHO, recommendations for influenza vaccine composition

science.claim: After 1492, diseases introduced from Europe contributed to a population collapse in the Americas of about 90% within roughly a century.
science.working: Koch et al. estimate about 60.5 million people lived in the Americas in 1492 and about 56 million died by 1600, a decline of around 90%, mostly from introduced epidemic diseases.
science.source: Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis, 'Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492', Quaternary Science Reviews 207 (2019)

science.claim: Beowulf, written in Old English about a thousand years ago, cannot be read by modern English speakers without study; its first word is 'Hwaet'.
science.working: The only manuscript (Cotton MS Vitellius A XV) is dated to roughly 975-1025 AD. Old English grammar, spelling and vocabulary differ so much from modern English that it is studied like a foreign language.
science.source: British Library, 'Beowulf' (Cotton MS Vitellius A XV)

science.claim: The length of the day grows by about 1.8 thousandths of a second per century, so after 974 years a day is roughly 17 thousandths of a second longer.
science.working: Historical eclipse records give an average increase in the length of day of 1.78 ms per century; 1.78 x 9.74 = 17.3 ms.
science.source: Stephenson, Morrison & Hohenkerk, 'Measurement of the Earth's rotation: 720 BC to AD 2015', Proc. R. Soc. A 472 (2016)

science.claim: In 1900 about 41% of the US workforce worked in agriculture; by 2000 it was 1.9%.
science.working: USDA figures: 41 percent of the workforce in 1900, 1.9 percent in 2000.
science.source: Dimitri, Effland & Conklin, 'The 20th Century Transformation of U.S. Agriculture and Farm Policy', USDA ERS EIB-3 (2005)
